newsitem.title: USA: Death cheats R.I. man who planned protest suicide.
newsitem.headline: Death cheats R.I. man who planned protest suicide.

text.p: Death on Wednesday cheated a right-to-die activist in Rhode Island who planned to commit suicide to avoid the final stages of a terminal illness.

Noel David Earley, who turned 48 on Christmas Day, never had the chance to test a state law banning assisted suicide. He died on Wednesday afternoon at his home in Lincoln, but not by his own hand, said a woman who answered his telephone.
Earley suffered from Lou Gehrig's disease -- amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, an untreatable, progressive and fatal neuromuscular disease.
Divorced and childless, the Vietnam War veteran had intended to test the state's nine-month ban on assisted suicide, but his condition worsened before he got the chance, the woman said.

On Sunday, Earley, who had planned to die by injecting himself with lethal drugs and kept a pine coffin at the foot of his bed, slipped into unconsciousness. He died of natural causes, the woman said.
"See that big muscle on your thumb," Earley told Reuters in an interview last month. "That's all I need to work." He then mimicked self-injection with his withered right hand.
He never revealed who would supply the fatal dose, though said he had been in contact with Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the top U.S. assisted-suicide activist.
"He said when the time came I should come to Michigan (where Kevorkian is based) ... But I found someone locally who would help me instead. Local is better," Earley said.
Earley, whose withered legs and left arm were paralysed by the disease, had become a spokesman for the right-to-die movement.

Last Spring, he testified before the Rhode Island Legislature, arguing that a law making assisted suicide a felony punishable by 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine should be struck. Instead the legislators revived and reinstated the law.

Earley and the American Civil Liberties Union were fighting to have the law declared unconstitutional in federal court. Earley's death "is a serious concern as to whether the suit can proceed," said ACLU spokeswoman Carolyn Mannis.
